prompt: In Standing's 1973 study, people viewed 10,000 pictures once each. Roughly how often could they later pick out the one they had seen from a pair?
options: About 83% of the time
About 50% of the time, which is chance
About 30% of the time
Every single time
correctAnswer: About 83% of the time
explanation: After 10,000 scenes shown for a few seconds each, people chose the picture they had seen about 83% of the time: far above the 50% that guessing would give.

prompt: Myth or fact: research shows that people learn best when teaching matches their learning style, for example pictures for "visual learners".
correctAnswer: False
explanation: Pashler and colleagues found virtually no evidence for the pattern that would show style-matched teaching works, and several good studies contradicted it.

prompt: A friend says picture tricks are pointless for her because she is "a words person". What does the evidence in this lesson suggest?
options: Pictures help across whole groups of people, and there is no good evidence that matching methods to a learning style helps
She is right: picture methods only work for visual learners
She should only ever use rote repetition, because words people cannot form images
Pictures only help people who have a photographic memory
correctAnswer: Pictures help across whole groups of people, and there is no good evidence that matching methods to a learning style helps
explanation: The picture advantage shows up across groups of volunteers, and the 2008 review found no adequate evidence base for teaching to learning styles.

prompt: Recall check: in the lesson's drill list (umbrella, lobster, trumpet...), the seventh word was _____.
correctAnswer: anchor
explanation: The list ran umbrella, lobster, trumpet, candle, bicycle, pineapple, anchor, volcano, scarf, telescope.

prompt: Match each study to what it found.

pairs.right: 10,000 pictures seen once; 83% picked out later
96.7% of pictures recognised against 88.4% of words
2,500 objects remembered in surprising detail
No adequate evidence for learning styles

explanation: Three studies of the picture superiority effect, and one review that tested the learning-styles idea against the evidence.

prompt: According to dual-coding theory, why is a picture usually remembered better than a printed word?
options: You tend to name a picture silently, so it is stored as both an image and a word
Pictures are always shown for longer than words
Words are stored in short-term memory only
Pictures are processed by the ears as well as the eyes
correctAnswer: You tend to name a picture silently, so it is stored as both an image and a word
explanation: Paivio proposed two separate systems, verbal and imaginal; a picture tends to get both codes, a word usually only the verbal one unless you picture it.

prompt: Find the step that misstates the research on why pictures win.
steps: Paivio's dual-coding theory says memory has separate verbal and image systems.
Paivio and Csapo found that asking people to image each word removed the picture advantage.
A rival account says pictures win because they look more different from one another.
Ensor and colleagues made words more distinctive with varied fonts, sizes and colours.
This made the picture advantage in recognition much larger.
explanation: Making words more distinctive did the opposite: the picture superiority effect in recognition disappeared, supporting the distinctiveness account.

prompt: You are learning a 20-item list. Which approach follows both the dual-coding and the distinctiveness explanations of the picture advantage?
options: Picture one particular version of each item, name it silently, and give each a detail no other item shares
Read each word aloud several times in the same tone of voice
Picture every item as the same plain grey shape so none distracts you
Only picture the items you find hardest and read the rest
correctAnswer: Picture one particular version of each item, name it silently, and give each a detail no other item shares
explanation: Naming and picturing gives two codes (dual coding), and a unique detail makes each image distinct (distinctiveness). Both theories point the same way.

prompt: The Rhetorica ad Herennium says memorable images should be "not many or vague, but..."
options: doing something
small and plain
written down
shown in black and white
correctAnswer: doing something
explanation: The Ad Herennium asks for images that are doing something: active images, in Latin aliquid agentes.

prompt: Myth or fact: the weirder an image is, the better it will always be remembered.
correctAnswer: False
explanation: The bizarreness effect appears mainly when odd items are mixed with ordinary ones; in all-bizarre lists the advantage disappears, and it seems short-lived.

prompt: You made every image on a long list as bizarre as you could, and a week later little of it remains. What does the research suggest?
options: Bizarreness helps mostly when odd images stand out among ordinary ones, and the advantage seems short-lived
You did not make the images bizarre enough
Bizarre images only work for visual learners
You should have used no images at all
correctAnswer: Bizarreness helps mostly when odd images stand out among ordinary ones, and the advantage seems short-lived
explanation: McDaniel and colleagues found the effect reliably in mixed lists; Zoller and colleagues found no advantage in pure lists and none after 48 hours.

prompt: Recall check: in the eight-item drill (kettle, ladder, goat...), the item that came straight after the goat was the _____.
correctAnswer: violin
explanation: The list ran kettle, ladder, goat, violin, mirror, cactus, drum, sandal.

prompt: Match each source to its finding or advice.

pairs.right: Crowns, purple cloaks, blood, mud and comic effects
Bizarreness effect reliable in mixed lists
No bizarre advantage in pure lists or after 48 hours
Funny sentences remembered better, even when expected

explanation: An ancient recipe and three modern tests of how far oddness and humour help memory.

prompt: Why, according to the Ad Herennium, is a solar eclipse more memorable than a sunset?
options: Because it happens seldom, and the mind is stirred by the new and striking
Because it lasts longer than a sunset
Because it is always frightening
Because it can only be seen with a telescope
correctAnswer: Because it happens seldom, and the mind is stirred by the new and striking
explanation: Sunrises and sunsets happen daily and stir no one; eclipses are rare and so a source of wonder. The author tells art to imitate nature.

prompt: Find the step that breaks the Ad Herennium recipe for an active image of a kettle.
steps: Make the kettle the size of a car.
Put a crown on it.
Leave it sitting still on a shelf so you can see it clearly.
Have it shriek like a whistle.
Let it pour hot custard over its own spout.
explanation: Images should be doing something, not sitting still. The other steps use size, costume, sound and comedy, all levers the lesson recommends.

prompt: Every image on your list is a giant: a giant kettle, a giant goat, a giant drum. Recall is patchy. What change follows from this lesson?
options: Vary the levers so each image differs from its neighbours: one moving, one muddy, one funny, one with a sound
Make every image even bigger
Drop the images and repeat the words instead
Use the same giant image for every item to save effort
correctAnswer: Vary the levers so each image differs from its neighbours: one moving, one muddy, one funny, one with a sound
explanation: Oddness works by contrast. If every image is strange in the same way, none stands out, so use the whole toolkit to make each one distinct.

prompt: On dual-coding theory, why are concrete words usually remembered better than abstract ones?
options: People are more likely to picture a concrete word, giving it a second, image code
Concrete words are always shorter
Abstract words are stored only in short-term memory
Concrete words are always more common
correctAnswer: People are more likely to picture a concrete word, giving it a second, image code
explanation: The chance of an image code falls from pictures to concrete words to abstract words; giving an abstract word a concrete stand-in restores it.

prompt: In the Ad Herennium's lawsuit image, the ram's testicles stand for the witnesses, through a pun on the Latin word testes.
correctAnswer: True
explanation: As Caplan notes, testiculi suggests testes, which also means witnesses; the cup stands for the poison and the tablets for the inheritance.

prompt: Match each bridge or kind of image to its example.

pairs.right: Gravity: a cup of tea on a grave
Justice: a pair of scales
Patience: an angler watching a float for a week
A whole poisoning case in one bedside scene

explanation: Sound plays on how the word sounds, a symbol already stands for the idea, a scene shows it happening, and a likeness of matter holds a whole idea in one image.

prompt: Recall check: in the abstract-word drill (freedom, envy, wisdom...), the sixth word was _____.
correctAnswer: honesty
explanation: The list ran freedom, envy, wisdom, luck, danger, honesty, comfort, ambition.

prompt: You need to remember the abstract word "democracy". Which image uses the sound bridge?
options: A demolition crew going crazy: "demo" plus "crazy"
A ballot box
A crowd raising their hands to vote
Saying the word ten times
correctAnswer: A demolition crew going crazy: "demo" plus "crazy"
explanation: A sound bridge plays on what the word sounds like, as the Ad Herennium did with Domitius for domum itionem. The ballot box is a symbol and the crowd is a scene.

prompt: What did the Ad Herennium say about using images to memorise exact words?
options: It is the harder task, best used as an exercise, after going over the verse two or three times first
It is the only proper use of memory images
It is easy, because every word has an obvious picture
It should never be attempted under any circumstances
correctAnswer: It is the harder task, best used as an exercise, after going over the verse two or three times first
explanation: The author treats word images as harder, rehearses the verse first so art supplements nature, and includes word memory as training for memory of matter.

prompt: Find the step that misreads the Ad Herennium's Domitius example.
steps: The author wants to remember the line Iam domum itionem reges.
He pictures Domitius raising his hands to heaven.
Domitius is being lashed by the Marcii Reges.
The image works because the name Domitius means home-coming.
Caplan notes that the play is on the form of the word, not its meaning.
explanation: Domitius does not mean home-coming; the name merely sounds like domum itionem. It is a sound bridge, as Caplan points out.

prompt: A friend offers you a book of ready-made images for 1,000 common words. What would the Ad Herennium author say?
options: That it is ridiculous: you will need images for whatever words come up, and your own images strike you more than someone else's
That it is the best way to learn the art
That 1,000 is too few and you need 10,000
That images for words are forbidden
correctAnswer: That it is ridiculous: you will need images for whatever words come up, and your own images strike you more than someone else's
explanation: He called collecting images for a thousand words ridiculous, said ready-made lists rob you of initiative, and told everyone to suit their own convenience.

prompt: In the link method, each image joins...
options: an item to the next item on the list
every item to a room in your house
each item to a number
the first item to the last
correctAnswer: an item to the next item on the list
explanation: The link method chains the list: item one interacts with item two, two with three, and so on, so each item cues the next.

prompt: Myth or fact: picturing two items vividly but side by side helps you remember the pair about as well as picturing them interacting.
correctAnswer: False
explanation: Wollen, Weber and Lowry found that interacting pictures beat words alone, while non-interacting pictures did worse than no pictures at all.

prompt: Bower and Winzenz compared four ways of learning word pairs. Which came out best?
options: Picturing the two things in vivid interaction
Making up a sentence linking them
Reading them in a ready-made sentence
Repeating the pair over and over
correctAnswer: Picturing the two things in vivid interaction
explanation: The ranking was imagery best, then sentence generation, then sentence reading, with rote repetition worst.

prompt: Recall check: put these items from the link drill in the order you chained them.
steps: rocket
piano
penguin
teacup
sock
kite
explanation: The full chain ran rocket, banana, piano, penguin, ladder, teacup, lighthouse, sock, wheelbarrow, kite.

prompt: Halfway through recalling a chain you blank on item 6, and items 7 to 10 vanish with it. Why?
options: Each item is cued only by the one before, so one broken link strands everything after it
Your memory can only hold five items
The images were not bizarre enough
The link method only works for lists of five
correctAnswer: Each item is cued only by the one before, so one broken link strands everything after it
explanation: That is the built-in weakness of the chain; stories and memory palaces are two answers to it.

prompt: Match each condition in Wollen, Weber and Lowry's study to its result.

pairs.right: Better than words alone
Worse than words alone
No difference in recall
The comparison group

explanation: Interaction was what mattered. Separate pictures actually hurt, and bizarreness made no difference.

prompt: Find the step that would leave a weak link in this chain for milk, eggs, bread and soap.
steps: Make the milk unforgettable: a fountain of milk.
Milk to eggs: the milk floods a box of eggs.
Eggs to bread: the eggs hatch and out march slices of bread.
Bread to soap: picture a loaf, then picture a bar of soap beside it.
Recall: start at the milk and follow each action to the next item.
explanation: The loaf and the soap sit side by side and do nothing to each other. Make one act on the other, such as the bread scrubbing itself with the soap.

prompt: Bower and Winzenz found that making up your own sentence beat reading a ready-made one. What does that suggest for your chains?
options: Inventing your own interactions is part of what makes them stick
Ready-made images from a book work best
Sentences always beat images
Effort makes no difference to memory
correctAnswer: Inventing your own interactions is part of what makes them stick
explanation: Their account was that memory benefits from actively searching out and generating relations, so build your own links rather than borrowing them.

prompt: In Bower and Clark's 1969 study, what median share of the words did the storytellers recall at the final test?
explanation: Storytellers recalled a median of 93% against 13% for controls who had the same study time.

prompt: Myth or fact: research shows that people who cannot picture things in their mind's eye get no benefit from memory methods.
correctAnswer: False
explanation: That has not been shown. People with aphantasia in Bainbridge's study leaned on words and placed objects accurately; how well image methods work for them is not settled.

prompt: Why did each control in Bower and Clark's study get exactly the same study time as their storyteller partner?
options: So the difference could not be put down to extra study time
Because the controls asked for it
So the controls could also write stories
To make the lists easier
correctAnswer: So the difference could not be put down to extra study time
explanation: Yoking the time means the six- or sevenfold difference came from what people did with the time, not how much they had.

prompt: Recall check: in the story drill (wizard, bucket, motorway...), the eighth noun was _____.
correctAnswer: castle
explanation: The list ran wizard, bucket, motorway, parrot, chocolate, iceberg, saxophone, castle, pillow, tractor.

prompt: Match each part of a story to what Bower and Clark said it does.

pairs.left: A theme running through the list
pairs.right: Organises the words

pairs.left: A separate story for each list
pairs.right: Less interference between lists
Guides reconstruction of a missing word
What the yoked controls did

explanation: Bower and Clark credited thematic organisation, reduced interference between lists and guided reconstructive recall.

prompt: Why can a story survive a forgotten word better than a link chain?
options: The plot runs through the whole list, so you can reconstruct what must come next
Stories are always shorter than chains
Stories use no images at all
Chains cannot hold more than four items
correctAnswer: The plot runs through the whole list, so you can reconstruct what must come next
explanation: In a chain each item is cued only by its neighbour; a plot gives a reason for every event and guides you over a gap.

prompt: Find the step that misreports Bainbridge and colleagues' 2021 study of aphantasia.
steps: Aphantasia is a lifelong inability to form voluntary visual images.
The congenital form is thought to affect around 2% of people.
People with aphantasia drew fewer objects from memory than controls.
They also placed objects much less accurately than controls.
They leaned more on words, for example labelling their drawings.
explanation: Their spatial accuracy was equivalent to the controls', and they made fewer memory errors. The difference was in how many objects they recalled.

prompt: A friend with aphantasia wants to learn a list of ten items. Which advice fits the evidence in this lesson?
options: Try a meaningful story, sounds and places, keep what works, and know the research has not settled how image methods suit aphantasia
Give up: memory methods cannot work without mental pictures
Only rote repetition can work for her
She must train until she sees vivid pictures before trying any method
correctAnswer: Try a meaningful story, sounds and places, keep what works, and know the research has not settled how image methods suit aphantasia
explanation: Bower and Clark asked for a meaningful story, not a film, and aphantasic participants used verbal and spatial strategies. The evidence is not yet settled.
